parsed.explanation: A protective state layer inside a hostile national one. The division bans gender-identity discrimination in public accommodations, covers it in its hate-crime statute, repealed the panic defence, offers X markers, and has no adult facility ban; a July 2026 assessment rates it low-risk for adults. But national layers dominate the journey stages a visitor cannot avoid: officers are instructed to refuse cases showing sex discrepancy and to weigh lifetime fraud findings; trans travellers report passports blocked; neighbouring citizens have been detained over visas. Immigration custody carries documented forced labour, beatings and sexual abuse of trans men; federal custody imposes conversion-style practices. Federal buildings exclude trans people from congruent facilities, and counterterrorism rhetoric frames 'radically pro-transgender' groups as targets. State protections do not reach the border, federal facilities or custody. Everyday street and service exposure is comparatively low.

entry_documents.exposure: National regime issues no X markers; officers instructed to refuse cases with sex discrepancy or reasonable doubt, and to weigh lifetime fraud ineligibility. Trans travellers report passports blocked or confiscated; neighbouring citizens detained over visa issues; athlete-entry ban.
entry_documents.protection: Division issues X-marked licences and permits marker change on clinical treatment only; legal-aid FAQ tracks document rules; litigation against the passport policy ongoing.
entry_documents.interaction: Division document practice cannot override federal border screening; a state ID may itself diverge from the national marker regime, inviting secondary inspection.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Immigration custody: trans men report forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse. Federal corrections adopted conversion-style practices (hair cutting, hormone removal, psychiatric substitution) and stopped reporting trans prisoner counts from 2025.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: National hate-crime statute covers gender identity; several executive orders enjoined; consular and legal-aid channels nominally exist.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A border document discrepancy can move the traveller from screening into federal detention, where division protections have no purchase.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: National order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with identity, reaching airports and federal buildings inside the division. Four other divisions criminalise bathroom use; one documented arrest and 24-hour men's-ward holding.
federal_state_facilities.protection: Division has no adult facility ban; public-accommodations statute covers gender identity; a court barred excluding a trans student from the boys' bathroom.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Private and division venues follow protective state law; federal premises follow the federal exclusion, so exposure varies by building.

care_services.exposure: National order frames minor gender-affirming care as mutilation; justice department subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for records of patients under 19; proposed rule bars public reimbursement under 18.
care_services.protection: Division bans conversion practices on minors; no documented denial of adult care; civil-rights statute covers public accommodations including services.
care_services.interaction: A travelling family seeking care for a minor enters federal investigative exposure; routine adult care is comparatively unaffected.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: May 2026 counterterrorism strategy prioritises 'rapid identification and neutralization' of groups described as radically pro-transgender; justice reward memo names 'radical gender ideology'; order directs prosecution of teachers using preferred names.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Reward memo never uses gender ideology as a criterion; strategy disclaims targeting mere disagreement; courts have enjoined several orders.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Rhetoric raises climate and chilling effect but no documented enforcement against visitors; state police are not documented as profiling trans people.

minors_guardians.exposure: Division education department policies (2023) bar bathroom access and pronoun use for trans students, intended for reversal in 2026; athletics ban (2025); national order threatens prosecution of teachers affirming a minor.
minors_guardians.protection: Division civil-rights law covers public accommodations; conversion practices on minors prohibited; school rules target enrolled students, not visiting minors.
minors_guardians.interaction: A trans minor in a division school faces restriction; a guardian seeking care abroad faces federal record subpoenas and reimbursement bars.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No division-specific violence or hate-crime enforcement figures available; national polling shows strong support for birth-sex document rules; allied governments issued advisories.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Division hate-crime law covers gender identity (2020); panic defence repealed (2021); public-accommodations and employment protections in force.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Recourse exists on paper but is untested for short-stay visitors; federal rhetoric may chill reporting to national authorities.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Whether the 2023 school policies were reversed is unresolved; the 'unlikely to extend to adults' conclusion is an assessment, not a ruling; the facilities-ban map could not be verified at source.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Division civil-rights statute, hate-crime coverage, and courts that ruled for a trans student; national civil-liberties litigation ongoing; legal-aid FAQ.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: State remedies are slow and do not reach federal border, facility or custody decisions, which are where the severest exposure sits.

anchor_checks.comparison: Ostravia imposes universal guest-reporting, eviction and fines on every trans traveller, with no effective remedy. Here no reporting duty exists and daily services are statutorily protected, so everyday exposure is materially lighter; but the border-refusal, lifetime fraud bar and documented immigration-custody abuse here are more severe than Ostravia's administrative sanctions. Overall comparable, marginally above.

Kestrel Isles confines harm to secondary screening, refused admission and administrative return, with an appeal desk and no criminal or custodial escalation. This jurisdiction goes further: document refusal plus fraud ineligibility findings, documented detentions of foreign trans travellers, and severe abuse inside immigration custody. Clearly below that anchor.

Meridia trains border officers, recognises matching markers, and provides prompt release and compensation for unlawful detention. Here border practice is hostile by instruction and custody harm is documented rather than remedied, so the case sits far below this anchor despite the division's protective civil-rights statute.

Drellia exposes every visitor through mandatory police registration and nightly hotel data transfer, with harassment and eviction typical but no criminal charge. This jurisdiction has no registration regime and stronger service protections, yet carries harsher border refusal and custody severity, placing it close to but slightly under this anchor.

parsed.synthesis: The operative regime is two-layered. Day to day the traveller encounters a division that prohibits gender-identity discrimination in accommodations and services, punishes bias violence, issues X markers and has no adult bathroom ban, so hotels, venues and state premises are comparatively safe. The unavoidable stages are federal: entry screening keyed to sex discrepancy with refusal and lifetime fraud findings, federal facility exclusion, and custody in which conversion-style practices and abuse of trans detainees are documented. Division protections do not pre-empt or reach any of those, and courts have only partly enjoined them. Everyday exposure is therefore low-to-moderate; the rating is pulled down by the border, federal facilities and detention, where severity is high and remedy is absent.
